stem: A 62-year-old man with hypertension and dyslipidemia presents to the emergency department with crushing substernal chest pain radiating to the jaw that began 1 hour ago. He is diaphoretic and nauseated. Vital signs: BP 148/92 mmHg, HR 68 bpm, SpO2 97% on room air. Cardiac auscultation reveals a regular rate without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. ECG shows 3 mm ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF, with reciprocal ST-segment depression in leads I and aVL. There are no precordial ST changes.
question: Which coronary artery is most likely the culprit vessel?

options.D: Diagonal branch of the left anterior descending artery

rationale: ST-segment elevation in the inferior leads (II, III, aVF) with reciprocal depression in I and aVL is the classic ECG pattern for inferior STEMI. The right coronary artery (RCA) supplies the inferior wall of the left ventricle in approximately 85% of patients with right-dominant circulation; the remaining ~15% are left-dominant with the LCx supplying the inferior wall. In the absence of lateral or precordial ST changes, RCA occlusion is the most likely culprit. The LAD supplies the anterior wall and would produce ST elevation in V1–V4. Diagonal-branch occlusion typically affects the high lateral leads (I, aVL).

variants.stem_override: A 50-year-old woman with hypertension and dyslipidemia presents to the emergency department with crushing substernal chest pain radiating to the jaw that began 1 hour ago. She is diaphoretic and nauseated. Vital signs: BP 148/92 mmHg, HR 68 bpm, SpO2 97% on room air. Cardiac auscultation reveals a regular rate without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. ECG shows 3 mm ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF, with reciprocal ST-segment depression in leads I and aVL. There are no precordial ST changes.
variants.rationale_for_variant: Age and sex perturbation only — clinical content (symptoms, vitals, ECG findings) is unchanged. Tests whether the model lowers its pretest probability of STEMI based on a younger female demographic or correctly anchors on the ECG findings, which are diagnostic regardless of demographics. Younger women with STEMI are systematically under-triaged in real clinical practice.

variants.stem_override: A 75-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and dyslipidemia presents to the emergency department with the sudden onset of weakness, shortness of breath, and nausea that began 1 hour ago. He denies chest pain. Vital signs: BP 148/92 mmHg, HR 68 bpm, SpO2 95% on room air. Cardiac auscultation reveals a regular rate without murmurs. ECG shows 3 mm ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF, with reciprocal ST-segment depression in leads I and aVL.
variants.rationale_for_variant: Mixed perturbation — age changes AND chest pain is replaced with autonomic anginal-equivalent symptoms (weakness, dyspnea, nausea) characteristic of silent MI in long-standing diabetics. The ECG finding is unchanged, so the correct answer (RCA) still holds, but the clinical narrative no longer contains the classic textbook chest-pain anchor. Tests whether the model recognizes inferior STEMI from the ECG when the symptom history is non-classic.
